title: Clinic patient: Alex, 28
learner_brief: Alex, 28, is waiting to be seen. Take a history, examine the patient, request any investigations you need, and record your findings, suspected diagnosis and management plan in the notebook. A tray with a measuring tape and wrist supports is beside the patient.

patient.name: Alex
patient.appearance: Young adult sitting on an examination stool.

catalog.summary: A young adult waits in clinic with a painful wrist after a fall. Take a history, examine the patient, request imaging and fit a support.

moods.calm: Mood: calm. You are relaxed and cooperative. You answer questions naturally in short sentences and do not volunteer worries unless asked.
moods.nervous: Mood: nervous. You are anxious about being here and about what this could mean. You speak a little hesitantly, with an occasional "um", and at natural moments you ask whether it is serious or whether you will be okay. Kind, clear reassurance from the student visibly calms you; if they are cold or rush you, you become more anxious. This changes only how you talk, never the facts.
moods.angry: Mood: angry. You are irritated about the long wait and about being here at all. Your answers are short and a little curt, and you may sigh or mention that you have been waiting ages. If the student acknowledges the wait, apologises and explains what they are doing, you calm down and become more cooperative. This changes only how you talk, never the facts.

avatars.male: You are a man: if pronouns come up, they are he/him. Your name stays Alex.
avatars.female: You are a woman: if pronouns come up, they are she/her. Your name stays Alex.

voice_context:
CASE FACTS (all you know as the patient):
- You are Alex, 28, an office worker, right-handed.
- Yesterday afternoon you fell off your bicycle after braking hard on wet leaves and landed on your outstretched right hand, palm down.
- Your right wrist has hurt ever since. The pain is on the thumb side of the wrist, near the base of the thumb.
- Pain is about 3/10 at rest and 7-8/10 when gripping, pushing a door, or when someone presses on the sore spot.
- There is slight swelling on the thumb side of the wrist. No visible bruise, no wound, no deformity.
- No numbness, no tingling, no pins and needles. You can move all fingers; gripping and pinching with the thumb hurts.
- You did not hit your head and did not lose consciousness. No other injuries apart from a small scrape on the right knee.
- You took one ibuprofen 400 mg last night; it helped a little.
- No previous wrist injuries, no chronic illnesses, no regular medication, no known allergies. You do not smoke.
- Your left wrist and left arm feel completely normal.
- You are worried because you need your hand for typing at work.
- You do not know what is wrong with your wrist.

result.patient_response: Ow! Yes, that's exactly where it hurts!
result.voice_context: [The student presses on the thumb side of your right wrist, in the hollow at the base of the thumb. It hurts sharply and you pull your arm back. React out loud right now in one short sentence, for example: "Ow! Yes, that's exactly where it hurts!"]

teaching.contribution: Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after a fall on an outstretched hand is the key sign that makes a scaphoid injury likely.
teaching.missed: The anatomical snuffbox was not palpated. Tenderness here is the key sign of a scaphoid injury.

result.voice_context: [The student presses on your right forearm, a hand's width above the wrist. It does not really hurt there. React out loud right now in one short sentence, for example: "That part doesn't really hurt."]

teaching.contribution: No focal tenderness over the distal forearm makes a distal radius injury less likely and localises the problem to the wrist.
teaching.missed: The distal forearm was not palpated. It helps to separate a distal radius injury from a carpal one.

result.patient_response: No, that side feels completely fine.
result.voice_context: [The student presses on your left wrist, the uninjured side. It feels completely normal. React out loud right now in one short sentence, for example: "No, that side feels completely fine."]

teaching.contribution: The uninjured side gave a normal baseline to compare the injured wrist with.
teaching.missed: The uninjured wrist was not examined for comparison.

scripted_dialogue.learner: Hello, I'm a medical student. What brings you here today?
scripted_dialogue.patient: Hi, I fell off my bike yesterday, and my right wrist has been hurting ever since.

patient_by_mood.nervous: Um, hi... I fell off my bike yesterday, and my right wrist has been hurting ever since. Is it serious?
patient_by_mood.angry: Finally. I fell off my bike yesterday, and my right wrist has been hurting ever since. I've been waiting ages.

scripted_dialogue.learner: What happened exactly? How did you fall?
scripted_dialogue.patient: I braked hard on some wet leaves and went over. I landed on my outstretched right hand.
Mostly around my right wrist, near the base of my thumb.

scripted_dialogue.learner: How bad is the pain on a scale from zero to ten?
scripted_dialogue.patient: About a three when I keep it still, but more like a seven or eight when I grip something.

patient_by_mood.nervous: About a three when I keep it still, but more like a seven or eight when I grip something. Is that bad?
patient_by_mood.angry: About a three when I keep it still, but a seven or eight when I grip something.

scripted_dialogue.learner: Do you have any numbness or tingling in your hand or fingers?
scripted_dialogue.patient: No, no numbness or tingling. It just hurts.

scripted_dialogue.learner: Is it okay if I examine your wrist?

patient_by_mood.nervous: Um, okay... but please be careful. Will it hurt?
patient_by_mood.angry: Fine. Just be quick, and careful.

scripted_dialogue.learner: I'm sorry, I know that hurt. I'll be gentle.
scripted_dialogue.patient: Thanks. It's okay, I just wasn't expecting it to hurt that much.

patient_by_mood.nervous: Thanks, that helps. It's okay, I just wasn't expecting it to hurt that much.
patient_by_mood.angry: Hm. Thanks. It's okay, I just wasn't expecting it to hurt that much.

result.title: Right wrist radiographs, four views
result.report: Bone alignment is normal. Joint spaces are preserved. No cortical break or lucent line is identified in the distal radius, ulna or carpal bones. Mild soft-tissue swelling on the radial side of the wrist.
result.image_credit: Illustrative example image only: a normal wrist radiograph (mirrored), by Mikael Häggström, M.D., CC0, Wikimedia Commons. It is not an image of this simulated patient.

result.title: MRI right wrist without contrast
result.report: Linear low-signal line across the waist of the scaphoid on T1-weighted images, with surrounding bone-marrow oedema on fluid-sensitive sequences. No displacement. Remaining carpal bones, distal radius and ulna are intact. Scapholunate ligament intact.
result.impression: Findings consistent with a non-displaced fracture of the scaphoid waist.
result.image_credit: Simulated report only. No example image is shown for this study because no suitably licensed image matching the case was available.

result.title: CT right wrist, bone algorithm
result.report: Fine non-displaced lucent line through the waist of the scaphoid with a subtle cortical break on the radial side. No comminution, no humpback deformity. Other carpal bones, distal radius and ulna are intact.
result.impression: Findings consistent with a non-displaced fracture of the scaphoid waist.
result.image_credit: Simulated report only. No example image is shown for this study because no suitably licensed image matching the case was available.

orthotics._doc: Educational fitting simulation. Dimensions are those of the virtual patient, not real-world sizing guidance.

diagnosis.name: Suspected scaphoid fracture
diagnosis.correct_text: Correct. A fall on an outstretched hand with anatomical snuffbox tenderness makes a scaphoid fracture the key diagnosis to suspect and exclude.
diagnosis.partial_text: Partly correct. A fracture is likely, but the specific concern here is the scaphoid: fall on an outstretched hand plus anatomical snuffbox tenderness.
diagnosis.incorrect_text: Not quite. A fall on an outstretched hand with anatomical snuffbox tenderness should make you suspect a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise.

next_steps: Complete the wrist examination: scaphoid tubercle tenderness and pain on axial thumb compression.
Request dedicated scaphoid-view radiographs; an initial X-ray can be normal.
If clinical suspicion remains despite normal X-rays: immobilise in a thumb spica splint and arrange repeat imaging or MRI.
Explain the plan and the risk of a missed scaphoid fracture (non-union, avascular necrosis) to the patient.

criteria.label: Mechanism of injury
criteria.met_text: You asked how the injury happened.
criteria.missed_text: You did not ask about the mechanism of injury (how exactly the patient fell).

criteria.label: Time of onset
criteria.met_text: You established when the pain started.
criteria.missed_text: You did not ask when the injury happened or when the pain started.

criteria.label: Location of pain
criteria.met_text: You asked the patient to localise the pain.
criteria.missed_text: You did not ask where exactly the pain is located.

criteria.label: Pain severity
criteria.met_text: You assessed pain severity.
criteria.missed_text: You did not ask how severe the pain is (for example on a 0-10 scale).

criteria.label: Associated symptoms (numbness / altered sensation)
criteria.met_text: You screened for associated symptoms such as numbness.
criteria.missed_text: You did not ask about numbness or altered sensation.

criteria.label: Examined the injured wrist
criteria.met_text: You examined the injured right wrist.
criteria.missed_text: You did not physically examine the injured right wrist.

criteria.label: Palpated the anatomical snuffbox
criteria.met_text: You palpated the anatomical snuffbox and elicited marked tenderness, the key finding.
criteria.missed_text: Critical finding missed: you did not palpate the anatomical snuffbox.

criteria.label: Checked a comparison area
criteria.met_text: You examined a comparison area to confirm the tenderness is localised.
criteria.missed_text: You did not examine a comparison area (uninjured wrist or adjacent forearm).

criteria.label: Recognised the significance of localised tenderness
criteria.met_text: You linked the localised snuffbox tenderness to a possible scaphoid injury.
criteria.missed_text: You did not show that you recognised what localised snuffbox tenderness means.

criteria.label: Introduced themselves
criteria.met_text: You introduced yourself.
criteria.missed_text: You did not introduce yourself or your role.

criteria.label: Asked permission before examining
criteria.met_text: You asked for permission before examining.
criteria.missed_text: You did not ask for permission before touching the patient.

criteria.label: Responded to the patient's pain
criteria.met_text: You acknowledged the patient's pain after the painful examination.
criteria.missed_text: You did not acknowledge the patient's pain after a painful examination.

criteria.label: Communicated respectfully
criteria.met_text: No disrespectful language was detected.
criteria.missed_text: Respectful communication could not be confirmed (no conversation recorded, or dismissive wording detected).

criteria.label: Considered a scaphoid injury
criteria.met_text: You correctly considered a scaphoid injury.
criteria.missed_text: You did not identify a possible scaphoid injury.

criteria.label: Recognised the need for further assessment and imaging
criteria.met_text: You recognised that further assessment and imaging are needed.
criteria.missed_text: You did not mention further clinical assessment or imaging (for example scaphoid-view X-rays).

management._doc: Separate dimension, NOT part of the 100-point total. Written against NICE NG38 (fractures, non-complex: consider MRI first-line for suspected scaphoid fracture) and common practice (immobilise and re-assess or image again when initial radiographs are negative). Not reviewed by a clinician.
management.title: Investigation and management

criteria.label: Requested appropriate imaging of the injured wrist
criteria.met_text: You requested imaging of the injured wrist.
criteria.missed_text: You did not request any imaging of the injured wrist.

criteria.label: Interpreted the imaging result correctly
criteria.met_text: You interpreted the imaging correctly: a normal first radiograph does not exclude a scaphoid fracture, and MRI or CT can show it.
criteria.missed_text: Your notes did not show the key interpretation: a normal first radiograph does not exclude a scaphoid fracture.

criteria.label: Planned immobilisation of the wrist
criteria.met_text: You planned to immobilise the wrist.
criteria.missed_text: Your plan did not include immobilising the wrist (for example a splint or cast including the thumb).

criteria.label: Arranged further imaging or follow-up
criteria.met_text: You arranged further imaging or follow-up.
criteria.missed_text: You did not arrange further imaging (MRI, CT or repeat radiographs) or a follow-up review.

criteria.label: Avoided unsafe reassurance after inconclusive imaging
criteria.met_text: You did not falsely reassure the patient that a fracture was excluded.
criteria.missed_text: Your notes treat the injury as excluded or minor. With snuffbox tenderness, a normal radiograph is not enough to reassure and discharge.

fitting._doc: Separate 20-point dimension, NOT part of the 100-point total. Simulated outcomes for an educational fitting exercise; not a validated sizing or competence assessment. Not reviewed by a clinician.

none.patient_response: There's nothing on my wrist yet.
none.neurovascular: Fingers warm and pink. Capillary refill under 2 seconds. Light touch intact in thumb, index and little finger. All fingers and the thumb move.
none.neurovascular_response: Yes, I can feel that, and my fingers move fine.

appropriate.patient_response: That feels snug and supported. It doesn't pinch anywhere.
appropriate.neurovascular: Fingers warm and pink. Capillary refill under 2 seconds. Light touch intact in thumb, index and little finger. All fingers and the thumb move.
appropriate.neurovascular_response: Yes, I can feel that, and my fingers still feel normal.
appropriate.explanation: Appropriate size, position and tension: the wrist and the base of the thumb are supported and the fingers stay free.

wrong_position.patient_response: It's sitting on my forearm. My wrist can still move and it still hurts when I bend it.
wrong_position.neurovascular: Fingers warm and pink. Capillary refill under 2 seconds. Light touch intact in thumb, index and little finger. All fingers and the thumb move.
wrong_position.neurovascular_response: Yes, I can feel that fine.
wrong_position.explanation: The support was not over the wrist, so the wrist was not immobilised.

wrong_orientation.patient_response: The opening is on the wrong side. It's pressing on my little finger side and my thumb is squashed.
wrong_orientation.neurovascular: Fingers warm and pink. Capillary refill under 2 seconds. Light touch intact in thumb, index and little finger. All fingers and the thumb move.
wrong_orientation.neurovascular_response: I can feel that, but the edge is digging in.
wrong_orientation.explanation: The support was rotated: the thumb opening must sit on the thumb (radial) side.

too_small.patient_response: Ow, that's really squeezing. My fingers are starting to tingle.
too_small.neurovascular: Fingertips slightly dusky and cool. Capillary refill about 3 seconds. Patient reports tingling in the fingers.
too_small.neurovascular_response: It feels a bit numb and tingly in my fingers.
too_small.explanation: The support was too small for the measured wrist circumference and compressed the wrist.

too_large.patient_response: It's loose. It slides around and my wrist can still move inside it.
too_large.neurovascular: Fingers warm and pink. Capillary refill under 2 seconds. Light touch intact in thumb, index and little finger. All fingers and the thumb move.
too_large.neurovascular_response: Yes, I can feel that fine.
too_large.explanation: The support was too large for the measured wrist circumference and did not immobilise the wrist.

too_tight.patient_response: That's too tight. My fingers are tingling.
too_tight.neurovascular: Fingertips slightly dusky and cool. Capillary refill about 3 seconds. Patient reports tingling in the fingers.
too_tight.neurovascular_response: My fingertips feel tingly and a bit numb.
too_tight.explanation: The straps were too tight: tingling and slow capillary refill mean it must be loosened.

too_loose.patient_response: It's the right shape, but it's loose. It shifts when I move.
too_loose.neurovascular: Fingers warm and pink. Capillary refill under 2 seconds. Light touch intact in thumb, index and little finger. All fingers and the thumb move.
too_loose.neurovascular_response: Yes, I can feel that fine.
too_loose.explanation: The straps were too loose to hold the wrist still.
